prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 1e-18

statement.case_for: After reading the full first-round exchange I keep B041 as my preferred configuration, now with more confidence than in round 1 because the attribution questions the chair raised have been answered in a consistent way. Six of eight members prefer it and all name the same pair. The citable idea is the magic-wavelength lattice: Katori showed that neutral atoms can be confined so that the light shift cancels, which makes many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation possible. Ye's group then took that regime to the 1e-18 level and used the many-atom clock as a physics instrument, resolving the gravitational redshift over millimetres, constraining variation of constants and searching for ultralight dark matter. That is a distinct step from the comb (2005) and from control of single ions (2012), provided the citation is written around the lattice clock and treats the comb only as enabling technology. Independent clocks now agree below 1e-18 across continents, so maturity is not in doubt. I also hold that the invention-versus-discovery question cannot be applied as a hard criterion, because the prize covers both and because the clock keeps producing measurements of nature. For me the remaining weight on the other side is that B029 is a discovery in nature, and I keep it as my first alternative.
statement.case_against: A third prize in precision spectroscopy after 2005 and 2012 can be read as incremental, and some colleagues will see a measurement capability instead of a new phenomenon. The pair also leaves out Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, who were decisive for particular accuracy milestones. Part of Ye's reputation rests on comb-based spectroscopy, so his credit must be argued from the lattice clock and the many-body clock work. The SI second has not been redefined, so some will say the culminating step is still ahead. I judge these points to be real but not decisive, and the first and third are handled by drafting the citation narrowly. If the committee instead weights discovery in nature above a clean allocation, B029 is where I would turn, but it would then force a contested cut among Halzen, Karle and Yoshida.

responses.point: Pearce moved IceCube to first alternative, says the AMANDA and IceCube drilling, optical-module and calibration teams make a two-person prize costly, and asks that the clock citation be anchored on the lattice concept with the comb as enabling technology only.
responses.response: We now agree on both points. On IceCube, I accept your instrumentalist argument that crediting Halzen and Karle leaves out the people who made the detector work, and together with the modest source significance it is why I will not put B029 first this year. I still think the diffuse flux is a discovery in nature, so I would not want it dropped. On Ye, I would settle your question this way: the citation names the lattice clock and its realisation at 1e-18, so his credit rests on the many-atom clock work and not on the comb. If the committee finds that distinction too fine, the right response is a narrower citation, not a third name.

responses.point: Kroll argues that 2005 rewarded the comb and 2012 the control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a many-atom regime that neither covers, and he disclosed a doctoral-period stay in John Hall's laboratory at JILA.
responses.response: I agree with the boundary you draw and I find the many-atom argument stronger than my own round-1 worry about overlap, so I withdraw that as a reason to hesitate. On your disclosure, a research stay in the laboratory from which Ye's work grew, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, does not seem to me to require recusal. I would ask that it stay in the record, as you did. The remaining point I would press is that the citation say 'lattice clock' explicitly. A reader who sees only 'frequency standards' will take it as a second comb prize.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the prize would be more natural after the SI redefinition of the second, and whether Katori and Ye cover the credit given the many strontium and ytterbium groups, and she says the soundness of the level-shift physics is something she can judge.
responses.response: I do not think the redefinition is a reason to wait. Agreement below 1e-18 between independent clocks is already the physical evidence, and a redefinition would be an administrative decision that follows the physics, not a prerequisite of it. Waiting also risks tying the prize to a calendar that the committee does not control. I do accept your point that the pair is not the whole clock community, and I rely on your judgement that the underlying shift physics is well understood, which is the part I cannot verify myself. I note that we differ on IceCube: low individual credit is a citation problem, not a lowering of its scientific importance, so I keep it as an alternative.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B017 as a field-creating discovery with a clean theory-and-experiment split, says the observations are stable after eight years, and acknowledges that if clean allocation is weighted above novelty then B041 is the right choice and she would not oppose it.
responses.response: Your last sentence is the heart of the matter, and I think the committee can say it plainly: the two candidates differ in weighting, not in facts. I weigh maturity and clean attribution more heavily this year because B017 still has an unresolved pairing mechanism, strong sample dependence and a credit gap for Cao, Fatemi and earlier twisted-bilayer theory that three names cannot close. I do not claim B017 is a lesser discovery. In my round-1 view the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiment is exactly the structure the prize rewards, which is why it remains my second alternative and why I would support it in a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B017 with a citation built on the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated phases, not on a mechanism, and says he would be content to see B041 prevail if maturity is judged decisive.
responses.response: I agree that any B017 citation has to avoid the pairing mechanism, and your wording is the right model for it. I take your offer to accept B041 as the real convergence point. I would add one qualification: you found the credit split among hundreds a main reason not to put IceCube first, and I now share that view, so on that we agree. On altermagnetism, your own statement that your recollection of the timeline is unverified, and the fact that nobody else ranked it, mean I cannot support it in this cycle without independent device-level evidence.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B003 to B041 and asks that the citation name the lattice clock explicitly so it does not read as a second comb prize, and he wants an answer on whether Katori and Ye are complete for the lattice concept.
responses.response: On wording we agree, and I have written the citation around the lattice clock and the magic wavelength to meet that. On completeness, I cannot show from the supplied text that Katori and Ye are exhaustive, and I would not claim it. What I can say is that Katori originated the concept and Ye's group set the accuracy and stability and developed the many-body clock work, and these two roles are separable from the contributions of the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups to particular milestones. Your own B003 case is the reverse: I still think it needs an explicit statement of which result it honours before it could be a configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice concept as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will want a wider clock citation that would bring in other laboratories.

Whether Katori and Ye are complete for the lattice-clock credit given the contributions of Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Hinkley and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups; I rely on the supplied credit and on memory for priority details.
Whether a later SI redefinition of the second would only confirm the case or change how members weigh it.
Whether the committee will weigh a discovery in nature (B029) above a clean-credit measurement invention, and how corroboration from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD would change the maturity of IceCube.
Whether the unresolved superconducting mechanism and sample dependence in twisted bilayer graphene will be settled enough in a few years to make B017 mature.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot, and I am a theorist outside atomic metrology. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye. I note Kroll's disclosed stay in the JILA environment and see no reason for recusal on that basis, and I also see no recusal need for any other disclosure listed in the chair summary.
